title: Application for a stay of execution of sentence of death

pages.text:
No. ______________
_______________________________________
In the Supreme Court of the United States
_______________________________________
In re Jamaal Howard,
Petitioner
_______________________________________
APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
_______________________________________
This is a capital case. Mr. Howard is scheduled to be executed
on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, after 6:00 p.m.
To the Honorable Samuel A. Alito, Jr., Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the 
United States and Circuit Justice for the Fifth Circuit:
Petitioner Jamaal Howard is scheduled to be executed by the State of Texas after 
6:00 p.m. central time today, Wednesday, October 7, 2026. He has filed in this Court a 
petition for an original writ of habeas corpus asking the Court to transfer his application to 
the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas for hearing and 
determination under 28 U.S.C. § 2241(b), as the Court did in In re Davis, 557 U.S. 952, 
952 (2009). Howard is intellectually disabled, and the Eighth Amendment forbids the 
State from executing him. Atkins v. Virginia, 536 U.S. 304, 321 (2002). No court has ever 
considered that claim under the clinical framework that now governs it. Pet. 1–2. Howard 
asks the Court to stay his execution pending its consideration of his petition.
A stay is warranted when there is a fair prospect that a majority of the Court will 
grant the relief the applicant seeks and a likelihood that irreparable harm will result from

the denial of a stay. Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). Both 
conditions are met here. Like the claim in Davis, Howard’s claim is that the State may not 
carry out the punishment at all; Atkins “places a substantive restriction on the State’s 
power to take the life” of an intellectually disabled offender. Atkins, 536 U.S. at 321 
(quoting Ford v. Wainwright, 477 U.S. 399, 405 (1986)). Pet. 6–7. The standards that 
inform the Court’s consideration of an original petition favor transfer: Howard’s present 
claim was not “presented in a prior application,” it rests on a framework that did not exist 
when his initial federal proceeding ended, and he makes a substantial showing that he is 
intellectually disabled. Pet. 7–11. The Court has also granted certiorari to review the Fifth 
Circuit’s reading of the “previously unavailable” requirement on which successive 
Atkins claims depend. Guerrero v. Johnson, No. 25-1003 (U.S. cert. granted June 15, 
2026). And without a stay, Howard will be executed before the Court can consider his 
petition.
As Rule 23.3 requires, Howard first sought a stay in the courts below. The Fifth 
Circuit denied his motion for a stay of execution when it denied him authorization to file a 
successive petition. App. A. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals denied his motion for 
a stay of execution when it dismissed his subsequent application, App. B, and today it 
denied a separate motion for a stay of execution by a ruling communicated to counsel by 
email, stating that no order would issue, App. E. No other court can grant the relief 
Howard seeks: the Fifth Circuit’s order “shall not be appealable and shall not be the 
subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari.” 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(3)(E).

Howard respectfully asks the Court to stay his execution pending its consideration 
of his petition for an original writ of habeas corpus and, if the Court transfers the petition, 
pending the conclusion of proceedings in the district court.
Respectfully submitted,
